Chapter notes:
   ●​ Language is orgnaized by size of the pieces it can be divided into from
      small to large

          ○​ Others are only for describing writing or only for describing
          speaking
   ●​ People speak in sounds NOT LETTERS

Arbitariness: there is no intrinsic relation between the form of an utterance (the
“signifier”) and what it refers to (the “signified”)

   ●​ No intrinsic relationship between a sound and its meaning (does this include
      words?)
   ●​ Sounds in different languages mean different things (sometimes there is no
       relationship)

Productivity (or generativity)

Composability: the ability to build new words and phrases out of smaller building
blocks.

   ●​ No problem with understanding all of the sentences; the sentences we hear
     and read are likely something that we do not encounter in day to day life.
          ○​  E.g., happiness, sadness



Openendedness: theres no limit to the number of words or sentences we can
create

Recursion: we can create complex phrases that have complex phrases inside of
them

   ●​ Ex. I heard the mai heard the mary heard that maho said this movie is good
          ○​ This movie is good - complete sentence
          ○​ Maho said this movie is good - complete sentence

○​ Sentences in sentences → embedding infinitely
          ○​ Limit is the ability to memory (working memory)

Displacement: no spatially present; hypothetical and false hypotheticals

   ●​ Hypothesizing about things that are known to be false



Duality of patterning: languages build units by combining meaningless building
blocks

   ●​ Meaningless but building things out of them from a second level



No conscious declarative knowledge; but knowledge that is able to become;

Native speakers: who learned it at a very early age, usually form birth (and to

 Chapter Review

Language as a formal and symbolic system

   ●​ Language can be described using abstract symbols and rules that specify
     how words combine into sentences.
   ●​ Linguistics also has strong historical connections to anthropology, including
      the study of language in relation to culture.
   ●​ During the 1950s and 1960s, many behaviorist psychologists opposed
      explanations that relied on internal mental structures or representations. The
      objection was to using these internal states to explain behavior.

Early computers and artificial intelligence

   ●​ Early AI programs performed tasks such as solving logic problems and
      playing chess.
   ●​ These programs raised the question of whether manipulating symbols
      according to rules could count as intelligence.

B. F. Skinner and behaviorism

   ●​ Skinner attempted to explain language through operant conditioning:
      behavior is shaped by its consequences.
   ●​ Reinforcement makes a behavior more likely to occur again.
   ●​ In VerbalBehavior, Skinner applied this approach to language, emphasizing
      the circumstances in which people speak and the consequences of their
      speech.
   ●​ Behaviorists emphasized observable behavior and environmental influences
      rather than explaining behavior through hypothetical internal mental
       structures.
   ●​ The note about “where a verb is” is incomplete; the broader point concerns
      objections to treating grammatical categories as internal things that explain
      behavior.

John B. Watson and the Little Albert experiment

●​ John B. Watson, rather than James Watson, conducted the experiment with
      Rosalie Rayner.
   ●​ They paired the appearance of a white rat with a frightening loud noise.
      Albert subsequently showed fear when presented with the rat alone.
   ●​ They also reported fear responses to some other animals and objects,
       interpreting this as stimulus generalization: a learned response extending
      to other stimuli.
   ●​ This illustrates classical conditioning, which involves learning an association
     between stimuli. Operant conditioning involves learning from the
     consequences of behavior.

Titchener and introspection

   ●​ The name is likely Edward Titchener.
   ●​ Titchener used introspection, in which trained participants reported aspects
      of their conscious experience.
   ●​ Behaviorists criticized reliance on these reports because private experiences
     were difficult to observe and verify independently.
   ●​ The specific example about reporting “how many chords” is unclear in your
      notes.

Internal states and experimental environments

   ●​ Behaviorists resisted using unobservable mental states as independent
      explanations of behavior.
   ●​ Controlled laboratory environments helped researchers study relationships
     between environmental conditions and observable responses.
   ●​ The comment about windowless psychology departments appears to be an
     anecdote about animal research facilities, or vivariums, rather than a
      general fact about psychology departments.

Skinner’s box and baby crib

   ●​ A Skinner box is an apparatus used to study operant conditioning in
      animals—for example, a rat pressing a lever to receive food.
   ●​ Skinner also designed an air crib to provide a comfortable, controlled
      environment for an infant. It was a separate invention, not a chamber for
      rewarding and conditioning his baby. Explanation by Skinner’s daughter

The Turing test

   ●​ A human evaluator communicates through text with a human and a
      computer.
   ●​  If the evaluator cannot reliably distinguish the computer from the human
      under the test conditions, the computer is said to pass.
   ●​ Natural language and deception are central: the machine must produce
      responses that lead the evaluator to identify it as human.
   ●​ Conversation also involves social context, making conversational ability
      relevant to discussions of social intelligence.
   ●​ Fluent language production raises the question of what evidence is
       sufficient to call a machine intelligent. Passing the test does not establish
      that it thinks in the same way humans do.
   ●​ Turing also proposed developing a machine with childlike learning abilities
     and allowing it to learn through experience.

GOFAI and the General Problem Solver

   ●​ GOFAI means Good Old-Fashioned Artificial Intelligence: an approach
     based on explicit symbols, rules, and procedures.
   ●​ The 1956 Dartmouth summer workshop brought researchers together to
      investigate artificial intelligence. Dartmouth history
   ●​ Allen Newell and Herbert Simon were central figures in early programs for
       logical reasoning and problem solving.
   ●​ Their General Problem Solver represented a problem through a starting
       state, a goal state, and permitted operations.
   ●​ The broader approach was applied to formal tasks such as puzzles,
     mathematical proofs, and algebra problems.

Tower of Hanoi

   ●​ The goal is to move a stack of disks from one peg to another.
   ●​ Only one disk may be moved at a time.
   ●​ Only the top disk on a peg may be moved.
   ●​ A larger disk cannot be placed on a smaller disk.
   ●​ The program compares the current arrangement with the goal and selects
      operations or intermediate goals to reduce the difference.

●​ This strategy is called means–ends analysis. An individual move may
      temporarily move away from the final arrangement to make a necessary
       later move possible.

Emphasis on formal problems

   ●​ Researchers viewed the mind as an information-processing system, with
      operations that could be described in computer-like terms.
   ●​ Early computers had limited input methods, such as punch cards, and
      required specialized programming skills.
   ●​ Problems with clearly defined symbols, rules, and goals were easier to
      represent than complex sensory tasks, such as recognizing a face.
   ●​ Researchers also treated rational, goal-directed problem solving as a
      central example of intelligence. Programs could represent a goal and select
      procedures for reaching it.

Skinner’s pigeon-guided missile project

   ●​ B. F. Skinner used operant conditioning to train pigeons to peck at an
     image of a target on a screen.
   ●​ The proposed system connected their pecks to the weapon’s steering
     mechanism.
   ●​  If the target image shifted to one side, the pigeon would follow it and peck
      at its new position. These pecks would guide course corrections, bringing
      the target back toward the center.
   ●​ The pigeon could track changes in the target’s position without
      understanding the weapon’s purpose.
   ●​ The system was never used in combat. The project faced skepticism and
     was eventually discontinued as electronic guidance systems became more
       reliable. Describing this simply as a preference for computers over pigeons
        is too broad.
